params.question: In the pathophysiology of PCOS, peripheral tissues such as skeletal muscle develop insulin resistance, yet ovarian androgen production rises. Which mechanism best explains this paradox?

answers.text: Ovarian theca cells remain insulin-sensitive; insulin synergises with LH to upregulate CYP17A1, increasing androgen synthesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Unlike muscle and adipose tissue, ovarian theca cells retain insulin sensitivity. Elevated insulin acts synergistically with LH to upregulate the cytochrome P450c17 enzyme (CYP17A1), dramatically increasing ovarian production of testosterone and androstenedione.

answers.text: Hyperinsulinaemia stimulates the adrenal cortex directly, raising DHEA-S and causing clinical hyperandrogenism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although adrenal androgens may be mildly elevated in some women with PCOS, the primary driver is ovarian — not adrenal — androgen production via theca cells that remain insulin-sensitive.

answers.text: Insulin resistance raises sex hormone-binding globulin, trapping more free testosterone in circulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Hyperinsulinaemia actually suppresses hepatic SHBG production, which increases the free (biologically active) fraction of testosterone — the opposite of what this option states.

answers.text: Peripheral insulin resistance increases GnRH pulse frequency, selectively raising FSH and driving follicular androgen output

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Altered GnRH pulsatility in PCOS favours LH over FSH (not FSH selectively). The key mechanism is the direct effect of insulin on theca-cell CYP17A1 activity, not a change in pituitary gonadotrophin secretion alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the vicious cycle: peripheral insulin resistance → compensatory hyperinsulinaemia → ovarian theca cells (which remain insulin-sensitive) respond to insulin + LH by upregulating CYP17A1 → excess androgen synthesis.

Well done. The selective insulin sensitivity of ovarian theca cells is the key to understanding why hyperinsulinaemia drives androgen excess despite peripheral resistance — and why reducing insulin levels (via weight loss or metformin) lowers androgens.

params.question: A 24-year-old woman has oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, and polycystic ovaries on transvaginal ultrasonography. Her serum prolactin, TSH, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels are all normal. Which condition must still be excluded before confirming a diagnosis of PCOS?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Hyperprolactinaemia is effectively excluded by the normal serum prolactin already reported in this patient.
Incorrect. Late-onset CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) is screened by an early-morning follicular-phase 17-hydroxyprogesterone level, which is already normal here.

Correct. Cushing syndrome can mimic every feature of PCOS (menstrual irregularity, hirsutism, central obesity, metabolic disturbance) and requires specific cortisol-based testing — 24-hour urinary free cortisol, overnight dexamethasone suppression test, or late-night salivary cortisol — none of which have been performed here.
Incorrect. Hypothyroidism is excluded by the normal TSH already obtained. Even subclinical hypothyroidism would be detected by this screening test.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion. Map each investigation to the mimic it rules out — serum prolactin excludes hyperprolactinaemia, TSH excludes thyroid disease, 17-OHP excludes late-onset CAH. Cushing syndrome and androgen-secreting tumours require separate, specific investigations.

Correct. PCOS requires both a positive diagnosis (2 of 3 Rotterdam features) AND exclusion of all mimics. A normal prolactin, TSH, and 17-OHP panel still leaves Cushing syndrome and androgen-secreting tumours unexcluded.

params.question: PCOS is primarily a reproductive disorder, and long-term metabolic screening is unnecessary once menstrual regularity is restored with treatment.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. PCOS is not simply a reproductive disorder — it is a chronic metabolic condition. Even when menstrual regularity is achieved, the underlying insulin resistance persists, conferring a 5–10 fold increased risk of type 2 diabetes. Ongoing metabolic surveillance (annual fasting glucose, 2-yearly OGTT) is essential.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. PCOS is a chronic metabolic disorder, not merely a reproductive one. Women with PCOS carry a 5–10 fold higher lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome is present in 30–40%. Annual fasting glucose and 2-yearly OGTT screening are recommended regardless of menstrual status.
